projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Leslie Gordon Blasius was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Leslie Gordon Blasius. Mr. Blasius served in the U.S. Army with the 11th Armored Division in the European theater. His highest rank was staff sergeant. I am Tom Swope, and this recording was made at Mr. Blasius' home in North Olmsted, Ohio, on November 21st, 2002. Gordon was 77 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941 when the war began for America?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Yeah, I was living in Millburn, New Jersey. I -- my folks had moved there a few years previously, and I was in high school at that time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of the -- December 7th, the day the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: I was upstairs. It was early afternoon, and I can remember hearing it over the radio, and I came rushing down the stairs, leaned over the banister and said, "Hey, Pearl Harbor's been attacked. We're at war." And at that moment, it didn't really sink in as to how deeply that was going to affect us. I was a junior in high school, so I had another year and a half before I was eligible to be drafted and inducted into the service. But in the meantime, I did enter the -- oh, you know, the volunteer corps that went around to make sure that all the shades were pulled, no light was showing, and people were safe, and that kind of thing. So we had just a little touch of that. But I think one of the things that really impressed me was the desire of several high school seniors to leave high school early to enroll in the armed forces in some respect, and one of my friends who was maybe a year beyond us, another group of friends, enlisted in the Air Force and was missing in action over northern Italy. He was an only child, and I can remember how devastated his family was at that particular time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Do you want to go on? Oh --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: -- okay. Well --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I'll continue. So you graduated probably, what, in --

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- June of '42 maybe?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: June of '43.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: '43? Okay.

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: And one week later the whole high school class of boys went down to the induction center. We were interviewed and checked over a little bit and decided which branch of service we wanted to be located in, and most of us were given our choices. And I went into the United States Army. And we had three weeks of furlough, was inducted -- or went into Fort Dix, and then was -- after the induction period, was sent immediately to California. So I spent, oh, about three months in -- waiting for basic training to start and then basic training and infantry, and then we were -- I was selected for the Army specialized training program, went up to Tacoma, Washington, for three months, then they decided that we were needed to fill out some of these divisions which were short of men, so we went back to California. We entered the 11th Armored Division. And that division had been in training I think for at least two years by that point, and we were then given our last, sort of, six months of testing and so forth in preparation for Europe, we were then entrained, went to New Jersey, and were shipped -- were supposed to go to Europe. We actually ended up in England, and we spent three or four months there before we were shipped over to France, and the battle --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Before we get overseas --

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- is there any -- no, that's okay. No, that -- I --

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Don't do this, but I think you've got it together that I can interrupt you. Sometimes I don't want to --

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: That's fine.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- derail your train of thought. But anything memorable during training, any memorable incidents that come to mind?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Well, they put me in a machine gun squad and I was probably, you know, 125 pounds, and to lug around a machine gun or a couple boxes of ammunition was almost impossible, but they just filled us in where we had to go, and we were at Camp Cook, California, and I guess the one thing that impressed me, depressed me, or whatever, was that when I was on KP one day and we had to go to the warehouse to pick up some food, I found out that the German prisoners who were at the camp there always got first choice in the food, and the U.S. Army got second choice as to what was coming out. At any rate, it impressed me that we were treating the prisoners of war so well, and I thought --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you find out any reason why they would have done that?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: I think only because they wanted the Germans to be sure to treat our prisoners, our -- the American prisoners, well, and they were treated well, didn't matter where they were. We very seldom met them, but at least we knew a little bit about them, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So about when did you go overseas, then, to England?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: We went in September of '44 and got there in October. It was a pretty rough crossing. We saw -- we were on one of the cruise ships which had changed countries a number of times. Can't remember the name of it. But I do recall that right behind us was one of these pocket aircraft carriers, kind of a ship from which you could launch a plane, but you could never retrieve one. So they were part of our guard along the way. As far as I know, we had no submarine attacks. But it was very cold. It was wet and windy. Fortunately, I was out in the -- out in the deck. That's where our platoon was billeted, and -- because in the interior of the ship was warm and hot, and as we went to meals and had to go into the interior of the ship, I was almost sick the first two or three days. So I would grab the orange or the apple, whatever they had for us to eat, and skip the tray of food and would rush back out on deck and get a fresh -- some fresh air out there. And so I -- we were sort of limited what we could eat the first few days, but I think we all adapted to it and -- and ended up in England. We were supposed to go, I think, to St. Nazaire to be stationed around a German submarine base there. They kept a division of soldiers, an archers and armor division, around that area, but for some reason they shipped us off to England. We were not expected there, and therefore the food supplies were rather low, and the first day I think we got a half of a hot dog to eat and that was our meal. So my particular squad decided, you know, we can't let this happen. We've got to do something. And we knew that around the area the English farmers were raising some vegetables. So several in our squad said, "We'll go and reconnoiter and see what we can find." So they got some fresh vegetables. And then I had a fellow in the squad, and I was just one of the privates who knew nothing, had no responsibility.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So your job was just you --

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Just being there right at that point.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Grunt?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: But one of the other privates said, "Hey, I think I could" -- "I saw some crows around. Maybe I could catch one." Well, I felt that was impossible, but before the day was over -- or the evening was over, we had the fresh vegetables; we had a crow. Now, what are you going to do with a crow, you know? Well, fortunately, one of the other privates, good friend of mine, had a father who was a butcher, butcher in Chicago, and so Tom said, "Well, I can butcher the crow." So he did. I didn't watch him do it or anything, but they put the meat and the vegetables and made a kind of crow stew. And everybody was a little afraid that they might get part of the evacuation system of that crow in his stew. But at any rate, we ate it; it tasted good. We had jokes from then on until the end of the war, you know, about the crow stew, but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How many guys could eat the crow?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was there enough meat for the squad?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Not really, you know, but, I mean --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: A little flavoring.

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: -- it was -- a little flavoring. It was just sort of a symbolic, you know, we're going to help out the Army and so forth.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So how long were you in England, then?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: We were in England from October till about the middle of December, so that'd be about two months. And then we were to ship to France. We got on a little boat. Terrific storm. They lost all the anchors, so we had to stay an extra two or three days on this little ship, and -- so they could put on one more anchor for us. And then we went into Le Havre, and the Battle of the Bulge had started while we were on that ship, and we were needed at the front. So after Le Havre, we got our -- they assembled our tanks and -- our group was in half tracks. They had armored artillery and so forth. So we were all pretty well mechanized, and we did 400 miles in four days, and someone said that's about the fastest that any group such as ours had ever gone, the most distance in the shortest possible time, and we -- I think it was about December 30th we became a part of George Patton's Third Army, and we were part of the group that came up from the south and helped to make the pinchers that cut off the Germans, and I think a part of our group even overlooked Houffalize at one time where the 82nd Airborne was located. So we were in the Battle of the Bulge for as long as it lasted. I think it was through the whole month of January, the really bitter cold, the snows and what have you, and we lost more men to frostbite and frozen toes and things like that than to any other kind of action.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any specific memories or incidents that you remember during the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: I remember that we -- we slept out for a month before we got under shelter, and it was a rough month, and we slept in -- well, they had, like, a light sleeping bag. It was almost about the thickness of a blanket, and we sewed in one more blanket. So we had two blankets, and -- remember how cold it was, and waking up a couple of mornings when we were really covered over with snow and had to sort of fight our way out. But I remember the -- something that's always stuck with me, it's the socks that I wore and how do we care for our feet, because feet I think were probably most liable to be subjected to problems. So we would have one -- wearing one pair of socks and another pair of socks in our -- between our helmet and our helmet liner so they could dry out. The third pair of socks we put underneath our arms so they could warm up and whatever. But any rate, we kept shifting socks that way, and that was one way to do it, to keep our feet.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first day of combat when you were actually under fire?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Yeah, I remember the first day. And as I look back at it, I can't imagine how stupid our officers were. You know, after all the years of training and what have you, we were -- they said, "Over the hill is a little town. It's just maybe a squad of Germans over there, so we're going to go and, you know, in the morning we're going to just take them out and secure the town and then move on to wherever division headquarters wants us to go." So in the morning we got ready, and I had a rifle and so forth and a box of ammunition, what have you. And they said, "Okay. We're going to go up the side of this hill and then we're going to go over the other side and you'll see the town down there and so forth. If there's any opposition, we'll just set up the machine gun or whatever." We went over that hill -- well, before we went, one other thing I think is important. We didn't -- we had winter overcoats, but they decided that since it was just going to be a brief two-, three-hour operation, we didn't need winter overcoats. So, you know, we just stripped down, in a sense, and went over that hill. We got over the hill and were on the downside when a half of a panzer division started opening fire on us. Well, number one, they -- we -- they sent the tanks up to the crest of this hill. You know, it's like shooting in a gallery, you know, at a fair or something like that, and they just popped off one tank after another after another, so there were no tanks left. And what did we do? Well, we who were the infantry part of it had to just lie down on the ground, take our entrenching tool, try to get a little bit of -- like a slit trench, get underneath the surface if you could a little bit. And at that day our squad leader was killed, our assistant squad leader was killed, and a number of other men in the platoon were killed there. And we lay out from about eight in the morning to about four in the afternoon. By that time our artillery had come up, the American planes had come in and were bombing and strafing and so forth, and we finally pulled back to the other side of the hill. Well, we got our overcoats on, as you can imagine, but that night we dug in three times. They kept moving us. So we spent all night, you know, digging slit trenches in this near frozen soil and so forth, and it was -- it was an experience, and I just can't imagine that our intelligence would be that bad, that our -- you know, you would expose, you know, companies of soldiers and tanks on top of a hill and so forth. And, you know, experience is the only way you really learn. And later on we could tell whether the artillery fire was ours or the enemy's. You know, we knew what to do or where to go and that kind of thing, and it made a great difference as we became, I guess you call, seasoned a little bit, and then a little bit more. But along the way, we always lost -- always lost men and that's the sad part. I was in combat a little over four months, and in that time I think there were only -- out of 250 men in our company, there were only four who remained at the end of that period of time, and I was the only one in my squad. Four were killed out of the original 12, and the others were either injured or -- one man had fought on Guadalcanal and he was so frightened of the whole thing that he just sort of took off. They had to evacuate him. So any rate, it was -- it was quite an experience.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have close buddies in the squad?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Yes. I had -- I had two very -- very close friends. They were both killed. It's hard even now to think about them. But the one fellow became the squad leader after that first day, and he and I -- you always had a buddy. He and I were buddies. Later on I became assistant squad leader, so he and I were still buddies. We'd still share the same fox hole or slit trench or whatever. And then he was killed during a -- well, we were going through Andermatt, which is a German city on the Rhine River, and what we were doing, the infantry, of course, had to go through all the houses and the apartments and so forth, make sure there were no Germans there who might become snipers or otherwise prove to be difficult. And so I took half the squad and he took the other half the squad. He got a little bit ahead of me, and there was a town square with a church in that square, and my squad got into the church and were about to go out the other side and enemy fire became a bit intense, and his squad came back, but he didn't make it. My other friend was -- we were in a line of fox holes in a hill, and they tell me he was in another fox hole at the other end of the line where our squad was. And his fox hole was the deepest, but a German shell happened to hit a tree and the shards of metal came down. He was hit and killed. And I did get to visit both families after the war, but it was hard to lose them in that particular way, but there are close friendships which are formed and those were my two close ones. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you find after that that you didn't want to get close to the replacements, or did -- it just happened anyway because you were in a situation --

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: No. We just -- we sort of went on and, you know, you shared with somebody else, you know, looking out for each other, if you want to put it that way, and -- no, we had actually been together, this one fellow and I, through our original basic training, same squad, ASTP, and so forth, and then had been put in the same squad, machine gun squad in the 11th Armored Division and so forth. So, I mean, we sort of grew together. And the other fellow, I don't know. He was -- he was in our group too, and, you know, it's interesting when you have some similar ideas or even some similar spiritual directions and that kind of thing, there are different things that pull you together, you know, things that you like about someone else and you have some affinity with, and so those were fellows that I got to meet, one from -- well, they were both from the Chicago area, and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you do anything with the guys for entertainment and to relieve the tension at any times when you were out there?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: You mean during the time we were in combat?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, when you're out there. I know you probably did not get shows, I am assuming -

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: No. We had some shows after the war --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- but not --

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: -- but -- well, I don't know. I didn't see him, but General Patton came to our outfit at one time and said -- we had, like -- I forget what it was. It was 37-millimeter antitank guns that you pulled along like the old artillery, and -- "Get rid of those pea shooters. They're no good." Any rate, so you got a little bit of the flavor of what he was like just on that one occasion, but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you get close to him at all to hear him or whatever?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: No, I never got --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Just heard about what he was talking about?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Yeah. That was -- that was about it, yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But perhaps did you -- oh, I don't know, I've heard stories about soldiers writing songs just to pass the time, kind of singing songs and writing -- making up songs, that sort of thing.

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Boy, we never did that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Didn't do any of that kind of thing.

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: You know, most of our -- our routine -- now, I can't say it was all exactly this way. Our routine generally when we first got into combat, we would start out on Sunday morning and we'd go through Friday night. We'd have one day to clean up, to oil up your weapons, to get all ready, and we had a chance to worship on Saturday. Some of us thought, oh, golly, we're -- you know, we're fitting in line to become good Jewish worshippers, but, you know, it didn't really matter at that time. But that was sort of our routine. And there wasn't time really -- you know, I mean, we never went back to any kind of an area. The only -- the only -- I had three days of relief one time, but that was because I got the GI so bad I just couldn't make it. So they sent us back to whatever the first stage is. I think it was a schoolhouse or something. And I -- I learned to take pills, because every two hours I had to take six pills, day and night. And, man, that stopped me up. And then I began eating again, and I can remember I was worried that I was either going to blow up or something was going to happen if I didn't get on a regular schedule again. But I -- but that's the only time that I had -- which was away from actually being in the combat zone. And I remember there was one fellow who came back and, man, he had a terrible wound in his foot, and I felt so sorry for him. And later on I found out he had shot himself so that he could get out of -- you know, get away from things. And it was interesting that he was the guy who in training camp talked about how he was going to really do the enemy in, you know, and he was the one, you know, and so forth. He was the biggest coward, and maybe -- maybe that's a sign of cowardice, the more you boast, the least secure you really are. And it was very interesting to find out a little bit more about personalities, about life, about people, and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was that unusual in your experience to see somebody that had inflicted a self-inflicted wound like that to get out?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: That was the only one that I knew of.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You talked about the one guy that snapped.

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: One --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You mentioned the one guy that was on Guadalcanal that had --

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- snapped from the stress.

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Well, he was -- he was sincerely frightened.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right, sure.

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: I mean, as we were going across France, there was -- a warning came that there were German paratroopers who were landing in the area, and this fellow could not sleep. He couldn't do anything. And he was genuinely frightened. I don't think that he could have stood up, you know. We would have had to carry him to the front or something, you know, eventually, but -- and I could see where that could happen. That could happen.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The stress of the situation, obviously.

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And that other fellow --

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- he thought that was his way out and, you know --

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- he couldn't express his fear, I guess.

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You said you were -- MR. SWOPE: Hi. FEMALE SPEAKER: Hello. MR. SWOPE: How are you? I'm Tom. FEMALE SPEAKER: Hi, Tom. There's some coffee on the dining room table. MR. BLASIUS: Okay. Good. MR. SWOPE: You said you eventually became the assistant squad leader; is that right? MR. BLASIUS: Yes. Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did that job entail?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Well, taking over if the squad leader wasn't present or unable to fulfill his duties. As I said, in the one town -- well, in fact, other towns too where we had to check out houses, I would take half the squad -- six, seven men -- he would take the other half, and then we would direct them -- one take one side of the street, the other another side of the street and we would -- we would do that kind of thing. But --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the procedure for checking out a house?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: You know, I don't remember. I'm sure there would be at least two men who would -- you know, one might enter and the other would follow if it were -- rooms were clear or something like, but I really don't remember. One of the -- now that you mention it, gee, it's memory long gone, but I used to have to be outside, you know, and one thing I loved is bread, and the Germans had this dark, black, solid bread which I just loved. So I would be out there with my knife or with my hands tearing off or cutting off pieces of bread and eating that while the men would go along the way and, you know, would be doing their work, and -- I don't know. I still love bread. Maybe that's the German that's in me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was it like when you crossed into Germany? What were the people like?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: The people were normal people, and I found out after the war, wherever I was, I would make friends with a family and -- during the war we didn't have a lot to do with the people, but I do remember we were in one town, one city -- and I can't remember the name of it -- where a warning came that it was -- some German civilians had said American soldiers had taken some of their jewelry or something of value, and word came down, "No way, Jose, you know. You got to treat these people with respect," which we did. We didn't see them often, but certainly it was -- we would -- you know, these were not for us the enemy. The enemy would be the troops or whatever equipment that we saw.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were they in fear of the Americans coming in, do you think? Did you encounter any of that?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: You know, I didn't -- right now I have no sense of that at all. You know, we were -- we did go through cities, but so often we were in the countryside and -- or in places where we didn't meet civilians. But going through the homes, I didn't think there was great fear. I didn't note that. I can't remember that at this point, no.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Again, it didn't always work, but they would try to tell their citizens about what the Americans would do. I guess there was some --

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: I suppose there was.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was there -- you know, you mentioned the rumors of the looting and that sort of thing. Was there a lot of souvenir collecting?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: There was some. During the war itself, there was very little that I saw. We were trying to stay alive. And after the war, immediately after -- and I was a part of this -- they called the Germans to bring their cameras -- now, there may have been other things, but they were to bring their cameras, you know, to a central station. And in this one city the American troops would relieve them of a camera or something and that -- I feel a little guilty because I was one of those who did that, and that was a -- it was not an expensive camera, but -- what do they call it? A reflex camera? And I used that for maybe 10 years after I got home, very, very nice camera, and I appreciated it. But there was -- I still have a number of German -- Army -- Nazi armbands, a symbolic short sword, and a number of other things. And I've showed them to my grandchildren, and if they're interested in it, they're quite impressed; otherwise, they say, "What's this stuff?" you know, "Super Man or whatever"? But -- so I have just a few things, but I -- one thing I did get which is a souvenir, after the war, we were on the Russian frontier for a while, but I do have a pistol -- never have had any ammunition for it, never have shot it or whatever -- which was -- which I traded a watch, wristwatch to a Russian soldier for this particular gun, which he had liberated, which was made in Belgium. So it sort of has an international flavor to it. But that's one of the souvenirs I have which keeps -- it's hidden away pretty much at this point.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any other memories of any specific actions in Germany before the war ended?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Well, no. We crossed the Rhine River on, you know, like a pontoon bridge. We went down into Austria, to Linz. That was our -- near the end of the war. One incident took place when we were stopped one evening and word came through that a patrol -- one of our patrols had been caught in a mine field and they're looking for volunteers to go out and bring these guys back. Well, I think almost everybody volunteered, but it was interesting that we learned later on that our chaplain was one of those went out. And they brought these guys back safely. 25 years later I went to a conference in Chicago -- I'm sorry -- and this chaplain was speaking -- ex-chaplain. So I went up to him, I said, "Hey, I was one of your GIs," and I said, "You know, you not only had services on Saturday and after the war, but you went out to rescue these guys, and" -- sorry -- "I can't imagine, you know, anything greater than that. You know, the Bible says greater love has no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friend." And I said, "You know, you were living that scripture out at that moment, and that really touched me and the others who knew about it." And he said to me, "You know, I felt as though my time in the service was almost wasted, that I never could see any results of anything that I did." He said, "You're the first one" -- "first one who ever came and told me that that service was meaningful to him." I said, "Well, it was, and I always wanted you to know." So, you know, sometimes God brings you together to a moment when you can share how much you've meant to each other. And I was always grateful that I had an opportunity to tell this man what he'd done had been meaningful to me and to many others. I suppose there are other incidents, but -- some of the things that happened after the war were even more interesting and more important to me than what happened during the war.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did that chaplain inspire you at all to go into your life's work?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Well, I was hoping this would come up somewhere.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: But I felt -- yes. It was a small, very small part, but I was going to state, even at the beginning of the whole thing, of our interview, that people said to me after the war, "Gordon, boy, it's a shame that you had to waste three years of your life." And I said to them, "They were the most important three years I've ever had in shaping who I am and what I was to become. One of the things it gave me is a sense of self-assurance." I said, "I was an only kid, my parents very loving, my father quite dominant. I really couldn't find myself, you know, because he -- he told me what was the best thing in my life here and there, what I should do." But I said, "I came to a quiet confidence in my own judgment, in the things that I could do and couldn't do and the choices I had to make. I think I could think more clearly, because I was on my own. My father wasn't there. My mother wasn't there. Nobody was there to help me or to guide me along the way. So in a sense I was on my own. And I felt in that experience, war experience, that I could stand on my own two feet." By the end of the war, I was a squad leader and I had -- at that point the squads were inflated. I had 18 men under my care. Their lives were my responsibility, and I felt if I could be responsible for them as well as for myself, if I could follow orders and yet had to make decisions within, you know, certain parameters, I was going to be able to do this in life, and that is something that is -- that gave me a quiet confidence that I had never had before. I was discharged just a few days before I was 21, went in when I was just beyond 18, but I said, "Those were three of the most formative years I ever had." The other thing it did, I think, was a part of my -- well, what should I say? -- progression to the point where I felt God was calling me to become a minister, and one of the things that has run through my mind has always been, out of all those people, why was I one of the few who was preserved, you know? How could my life count for something in this world? You know, what should it become? And I had no idea. And it was -- gee, it was probably three, four years later that I felt I was called to the ministry, but, you know, it's gone far beyond that. That's the call; that is, called to serve other people, to be understanding of even our enemies. And I think after the war when I had a chance to come to know German people, civilians, that I found that, you know, they're real people who have real needs, real aspirations, and many of them loved to serve the same God, and, you know, there's a tie that brings you together with others. And there are many people I don't understand in today's world. Their lives and their cultures and their religion is so different. But I do know they are a creation of God and it gives me some respect for other people in that way and a desire in my own life to see, you know, how can I serve or how can I help other people. So it's been sort of a -- those three years were really so important to me and they've sort of given me some direction into what I've done, what I've become, my appreciation for life, for nature, my, really, dislike for war -- and I don't say that war is -- you know, can always be avoided, you know, conflict, but I do say that there are many other ways we should try; otherwise, you know, they're going to be somebody else's son or brother or friend who's killed, and even though I don't know those people, don't understand their culture and so forth, I know that there is a human tie that is very, very important, a tie that, you know, all of us should be respecting.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember VE day? Where were you on --

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- VE day?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: I was at a farmhouse in Austria, and by that time they had allowed us to bed down in houses. I think just a few days before there had been snowfall -- we were out in the country somewhere. I never knew where I was, actually, and even at the end of the war, we were in Austria, we were at a farmhouse, we were in the country, but it was just -- during the war my dad would send me, you know, a little map and an article about where the 11th Armored Division was, and he'd mail that over to me, and as we were going, I'd open that -- up his letter, I'd say, "Oh, here we are, fellows," or "here's where we were last week," you know, or whatever. We had no idea where we were or what we were doing. But we were in this farmhouse and a great sort of celebration and -- that this was the end. There was really no special way that we could celebrate. We were just -- they called us -- eventually I'm sure they called us together and -- you know, our units and so forth and we didn't have to be on patrol in that particular way as we had been in the past. So we could do other jobs, which we did at that point.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any other memories of letters or packages from home?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Awful lot of VE mail went back and forth. My mother, I think, put together a package every day that I was overseas, and when we had one-a-week mail call on that Saturday, I would get six or seven packages, and I had the whole squad around me at that point, because we had -- you know, oodles of cookies. We had some canned food and things like that, everything to eat, of course, and everybody loved -- loved Gordon at that particular moment, but it was -- those were -- those were nice -- nice moments when we could share. But really the letters from home and -- were really what kept us alive and made us -- made the -- you know, made that time during the war worthwhile.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things would they write to you?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Probably only things that were happening around the house or the community or the church. Mother was a church organist and choir director and Dad was active, so we'd always want to know. And sometimes some of the other fellows who were from the church, there would be news about their wartime activities or where they were or something like that, and -- but family news was probably most important, somebody has a cold or whatever it might be, and that's what we were interested in.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you able to write much back to them at all?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Well, all we wrote was censored, of course, and so we made things very general. I didn't know where I was. They knew more about where I was, and I really couldn't say, you know, any specific things about what we were doing, that kind of thing, but -- I can't remember what I wrote. But do you know my dad died three years ago and -- I was an only child. In the attic we found every letter that I had written to him when I was in service. Now, I've done something that is unpardonable. I took only four or five letters from each year and kept those. The rest we destroyed. And I know my sister-in-law said, "Gordon, you ought to keep those." I said, "What am I going to do with them?" "Some day somebody's going to write someday." I said, "It isn't worthwhile." But it was interesting to go back and to look at some of those letters and to do some memory recalling those days. Something I have started, though, I decided four or five years ago, I'm going to write my story, it's called, and so -- I don't even call them chapters. I just call them incidents. And I was asked with Jerry Kennard, whom you've interviewed six weeks ago or so, to -- he and I were to tell something to a women's club about our experiences. So I had written up three or four incidents, which could be one page, could be three pages long, of things that happened to me. END OF SEGMENT 1 [INTERRUPTED]

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you actually link up with the Russian troops, then?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Yes. Well, yes, we were on a border and we didn't make the preliminary link. Some of the men in our platoon did. I wasn't in on that part of it, but we were actually on the Russian frontier or frontier with Russia at the time that the iron curtain had came down. Very interesting.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Much encounters with any of the Russian soldiers?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Yeah, we had a couple things. One -- we were sent out to guard a small hospital in the -- some beautiful rolling country land of Austria. Went out there, found out there were two or three doctors; there were no nurses. "Why were there no nurses?" I inquired. Well, because the Russians had come in and not been gentlemanly with the women, so they had taken off, gone behind the American lines. So I sent my half track. They brought, I don't know, a dozen Russian nurses -- or Austrian nurses back, and the hospital began to operate as it was supposed to. One day my -- some guys in my squad, a half dozen of them, said, "Sarge, we'd like to go out and do some hunting." I said, "Oh, come on." Well, "Come on. Just let us" -- "you know, we might find some fresh meat or something, or at least, you know, get some exercise," whatever. So I let them go, reluctantly. While they were gone, a Russian officer drove up and -- just his driver and himself, and he said -- well, first of all, we had communication, which was interesting. There was a man who spoke Polish and Russian. We found somebody who spoke Polish and German, and that fellow could also speak English, so we had a conversation going back and forth that way. And he -- the Russian officer said, "I command that you give me all of your blankets at this hospital." I said, "No way. Those blankets are for the people who are ill here and we can't give you any blankets at all." "But I demand it." I said, "No, no way." So he got out of the Jeep and sat on the side of a bank overlooking a little valley down below, and I sat, you know, 50 feet away, and just going to wait each other out, I guess. At any rate, looking down below you could see some open fields and then some patches of forest. All of a sudden out of the forest, one patch of forest, came a half a dozen deer. They were running like mad, and about 10 seconds later came six GIs. They started shooting and they shot every one of those deer. The Russian officer saw that, got into his Jeep, and drove away, and we never had any more problems that way with him. There were other problems later on. But we were able to secure this hospital until, you know, others came in the next week and took over that job. Another time we were put on the Russian frontier on a railroad line, and, okay, the Russians are over there. There are about three or 4,000 of them in a small town in a billeted area. And so I had 16, 18 men, half track, you know. And this railroad line was the dividing line. Well, the first morning about 2,000 Russians came over the dividing line and marched past us. Somehow I found out that one of the colonels could speak French and I could speak a little French, high school French at that time, and I found out -- you know, I asked, "Pourquoi?" you know, "Why are they coming over here?" And he said, "Oh, we got all our horses billeted over here, plus we have a rifle range over here." So every morning these people went back and forth. Well, I said, "Well, let's be friends and" -- any rate, they brought some vodka and my men had some -- you know, a couple bottles of whatever they gave us, and they traded them. So one night was a night when the Russian colonel and our men had time together to enjoy some socializing. The next day he rode by and didn't even turn his head, wouldn't give me a greeting at all. And I was able to catch his attention on the way back, and he told me, "We have been given orders not to speak or recognize the American soldiers." And that was the beginning of the iron curtain where we were. I called up the officer in charge, and I said, "Hey, you know, here's our situation." I said, "What should we do?" "Just hang in there. We're right behind you," he said. And I knew he was 20 miles behind us. But at any rate, he was behind there with something. And we finished our tour of duty in that spot and we took off.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So both these stories were after VE day when you [_+5:47]

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: This is after VE day, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Getting back to the deer story --

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- when he left, was he impressed with their marksmanship? Is that why he left?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: I think so. He knew we had live ammunition, that we could shoot, and he was -- you know, I think he respected that. Yeah, they pulled something else too. They sent somebody up to the hospital late one afternoon, early evening. And I didn't know it, but they had brought a report that somebody had been injured and they needed a doctor right away, and, of course, my men said, "Oh, yeah, sure," and they got a doctor and he walked down the road with him. I found about it. I said, "Oh, my gosh. You didn't let him go, did you?" So I sent three of my men with armed rifles. "Go after them as fast as you can go," and they went down that road, and they saved that doctor shortly before he was going to be executed. And, you know, you just -- some of the other things I won't tell you about that -- stories of what happened when the Russians were in that area, but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, you're welcome to share them with the Library of Congress.

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Yeah. Well, it's very fright -- well, 70-year-old -- woman in her 70s was raped and killed and her husband was also murdered. We found out, you know, of course, after it had happened, and, you know, these are things that, you know, are really to us -- even at that point were barbaric. We were very hardened to -- you know, to injury and other things, but, you know, underneath the surface I felt -- I feel that during the war we really did try to, say, preserve the civilians or to do things militarily decently and in order, if I put it that way. But we found that -- another case when the Russians -- we were on the border when they -- they were to leave a town and we were to occupy it. They said, "Well, we had" -- "we need until tomorrow to leave." So okay. We withdrew and came back the next day. By tomorrow, they had taken every movable object in that town. The stores were completely empty. The houses were empty of furniture. Anything that they could take they took. Mostly they had horse-drawn vehicles, and there were some women, Russian women in the infantry there also. So it gave us a completely different view of, let's say, our Russian allies. But, you know, when you think of it, they'd gone -- they went through so much during the war, they suffered so many casualties, it was just brutal, and I -- you know, I can see where you would become so hardened that any kind of positive veneer would be pushed away and, you know, just -- you would just try to survive and take anything that you could. And it's unfortunate that it was that way, but they probably didn't have enough food to go on and, you know, they had to take food as they moved from place to place, so forth. So any rate --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you in Patton's Third Army the whole time, then?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Yeah. Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you involved at all in liberating any of the concentration camps?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Oh, yes. I -- not me personally, but I think it was Mauthausen and I believe there was one other. Yes. And we just had a reunion, 11th Armored Division Association reunion, this summer and they were talking a bit about it. But, yes, elements of our group went to Mauthausen. We were the first allied troops who were there. And one thing that I -- that I remember about it is the fact that somewhere there was a bulletin board, not long after this -- the -- our troops had gone there, and I can see, you know, on a, say, 11-by-17 print -- I can see how the -- the prisoners had been executed, laid -- how they were laid out in stacks, piles of bodies, naked bodies that were out there. I can't tell you now how high. 6, 8, 10 feet, and just -- just bodies. And it really made you shudder to think that, you know, this kind of inhuman treatment could take place, but it did. And so when I hear some -- some rumors or write-ups about people saying, "Oh, that was only" -- you know, "That wasn't real. That's just in your mind," I can say, "Well, I wasn't there, but there are men in our outfit who were there who took pictures and helped." And there was a very interesting little story that -- I can't remember it completely, but someone wrote to our -- the magazine that comes out for our division association saying they had survived -- this person had survived Mauthausen, had been shown courtesy and helpfulness, gotten medical attention and food and some clothing and put in the right hands, and had survived at the end of this thing and wanted to thank these Americans of the 11th Armored Division who had come in and made this possible. And, you know, a testimony like that I think says something, says something to me: Hey, it really happened and we really did have a sense of compassion in wanting to be -- to bind up the wounds that had been caused there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How long were you in the occupying forces over there, then?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Well, VE day was, I think, May 5th, and about February -- the beginning of February the next year I was in the occupying -- Army of Occupation. And we would -- oh, I don't know, they -- they'd get us up in the middle of the night -- it was Saturday night -- and send us to some town where we'd get there at five in the morning and go through and looking for pistols or rifles or contraband or something, and mostly that was without any success, if you want to say getting -- getting weapons was concerned. There were a lot of, gee, refugees -- no, not refugees -- people who had been imported, you know, like Poles and others.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Displaced persons.

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Yeah. Well, they had been brought in, you know, to bake the bread, to do all the menial jobs, and we found a lot of them in, like, schoolhouses and other buildings where they had multilevel bunk beds and things like that, and we had to check out some of those and so forth and -- it was hard for them. The first troops that -- well, what should I say? Prisoners. I don't know where they were from. Could be Polish troops or whatever. But we sent them back and we learned that these prisoners of war when they got off the trains had been shot, decimated by the Russians, and so we never sent another, you know, prisoner -- German prisoner or whoever it was back to their homelands until -- well, we didn't send them back. I don't know when. Because there was probably a Russian occupation, you know, and has been for many, many years. But it -- it's sort of sad, I mean, the feeling of vengeance and what have you.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Is there any possibility that you would have been sent to the Pacific after VE day?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Very strong possibility. As you know, we all gained points, so many, you know, years or months in service, so much time overseas, how many battle stars, have you been wounded, and all this kind of thing, and I remember 52 was my number. Well, they sent home the fellows who had the highest numbers, and I envied them because they were going home for a month, you know, before they got sent to the Pacific. Well, near the end of the war in Japan, we started saying, "Aha, they're not going to waste their time and their boat space. They're going to ship us all right over there." And there was -- there was some talk and a bit of -- sense of frustration or fear that we would be involved in that without ever seeing our families again. And so if it had happened, it had happened, but fortunately May to August, three months, brought the end of the war for us.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Remember hearing the news that they had dropped the bomb?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: You know, I don't recall that particularly specifically, no.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You just knew it was over?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Well, I'm sure we heard it and we rejoiced because we figured at that point we would not be going back -- or going -- you know, taking the long way around to the Japanese, to the Pacific theater of operations.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you finally got home in, what, February of '46?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: No, actually it was March. Took us a long time. We were in one of the cigarette camps, Philip Morris or whatever it was, in France, and, of course, they had to install new boilers in the ship because they had gone bad. That was, I think, a three-week additional wait there, and it just seemed to be forever. Yeah. But we -- we made it back.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you finally got back?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: It was great. My father worked for the New York Telephone Company, and during the war he had worked directly, oh, in communications with the warships and the transports and so forth which came into New York Harbor. He was one of those who helped set up the communication systems with them. So he had -- was privy to information. He knew which ship we were coming back on. He knew where we were going to dock, and it was in Hoboken. And there was my mom and dad. It was a great, great thing. I remember they had brought me food, you know. "What would you like?" Got cookies and, you know, other things. I said, "Do you have any bananas? I haven't seen a banana in 18 months." Well, they had five or six bananas. I'll tell you, I put those under my coat. It was cold and we had our winter coats on -- under my coat. And on the train on the way down to -- I can't remember. It was Camp Kilmer, I think, we were going to be discharged. I sneaked out one of those bananas, and, boy, I just ate a little bit at a time all the way back to Camp Kilmer. That was -- that was heaven, near heaven. So --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You sneaked the banana. Were you afraid someone would have [_+17:42]

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Yeah, I didn't want to share my bananas with anybody else, and I didn't, which was sort of a nasty thing, but -- but I did. One thing was interesting. The reunion this summer of our division, there was a fellow there who was also a friend -- not a close buddy, but a friend all through, right from the beginning, you know, from our first induction. He lives in Eastern New York State. At any rate, he and I were in the same -- you know, in the same squad, training squad. We sat side by side when we were discharged. Now, I don't know how many times that can happen where you spend nearly three years, you know, with a guy going, you know -- being in the same outfit and all that kind of thing. So we had some good thoughts, some good things to share together, and -- but it was great to be discharged and find a new civilian life.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have any trouble adjusting to civilian life after that?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Not really, no. It was in the spring, and one thing I had always -- you know, I guess you set goals for yourself. I always wanted to learn how to type. So I went up to the high school and I said, "Hey, could I learn to type?" They said, "Sure. We'll put you in a typing class." The teacher there said, "Here's a book. You can read. You go ahead and do it, and if you need help, let me know." I'm not a very good typer, but I type all the time. That's -- that's something I do. Then my dad had saved his vacation. We went to the west. He spent -- we spent six weeks going through, oh, Colorado, Wyoming, Washington, Oregon, California, and some of the states out there, and then down through Arizona or New Mexico and so forth. And that -- that caught my fancy. And so my first job was in Colorado, and probably after we retired, we would have gone out there except my wife likes the Jersey shore and I like the mountains, so we decided we'd stay here where our friends are.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you think about that experience overseas, does one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Well, when we were in England for two months before we went to the continent, we got about three passes. Two of them were to London and one I think I got to Bristol. But while we were in London we went to -- we stayed with the Red Cross, and they're known for more than doughnuts and coffee. They're also known for having beds and sheets. I slept between sheets for the first time, I think, since I got in the Army, except for one furlough when I went home. And -- I don't know. That was the most contended feeling, I think, that I had. And it's not much of a high moment, but it was for me, home comfort if you want to call it that. It was really great. And I appreciated the Red Cross and all that they did. It was very helpful, very meaningful. Not a big touch, you know, but a touch which sort of sets off your life with a couple little colors here that make it worthwhile and make it seem better than it is, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That was probably the last time you slept in a good bed for quite a while; right?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You didn't do that when you were in mainland Europe?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: No. I was trying to think of -- now, they would put us in barracks or schools or some other place --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Cots?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: -- along the way. Yeah, cots pretty much, yeah. It was sort of makeshift, but, you know, you got used to it, and some of my work here in the church has been going on these youth work camps. Hey, we've slept on floors, you know, we slept on couches. We slept on the ground lots of times, that kind of thing, and made it possible just to, I don't know -- I can go to sleep now and go to bed. I am so tired, you know. And I found that I learned that in the Army. I was always tired. So if you got five minutes, didn't matter where you were. You slept sitting up, standing down -- standing up, sitting down, lying down, whatever. It didn't matter where it was, and can do that today yet, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Well, just a little funny thing I think. We were inducted -- well, before -- yeah, we were inducted and then we had to go -- we had three weeks of furlough before we had to go down to Fort Dix. My name began with B and I was the first name on the list. And any rate, there was a list of fellows who were going on this bus, and I was made, what, a temporary corporal or whatever it was. It was very temporary. But I was in charge, my first rank. And we were getting on the bus and the local committee draft board was there, my folks were there, and before the door closed -- and I was standing on the step -- I can remember the head of the draft board yelling out, "Give 'em hell, Blasius. Give 'em hell." And my folks' face dropped, you know. Ooh. We don't use that word. And I can -- I can remember that so distinctly. And during the war while I was in the service, I used lots of words, bad words, and before we came back from overseas, I can remember that we formed a club, about four of us who were going back, and we decided if we said any word, you know, we had to put in 25 cents every time we said it. And that helped us a little bit, helped us quite a bit as we got back home, because I really didn't want to use hell and damn or anything else with my folks. And those were everyday words that we used all the time when we were in the service, as you know. Yeah. I can't remember a lot of things. Visiting my aunt after the war, she had a visitor coming from England, and this lady said, "You don't know me, but your aunt has told me about you." I think I was one of the favorite nephews. Any rate. But she said, "I prayed for you every day." And I was thinking, Is that why I came through? you know. I don't know. We prayed for people who didn't make it. It's a very -- you know, some really good people. And I used to ask myself, why did all the people who, you know, didn't care about God, how come they got through and a couple of my friends who, you know, were really good Christians didn't make it? So I don't know. I don't know. But the Army experience taught me so many things. I got to -- I was thinking later on -- you know, I told you you choose friends because you have certain affinities. And one was a Jewish boy. We did a lot of things together when we were in ASTP, and there are a lot of things we didn't like. I mean, we didn't drink and we didn't -- you know, a lot of other things. But we liked movies and we liked to take walks and enjoy nature or look at the houses or whatever, and -- that were in the area. And there was another boy, Ralph, and he was a very staunch Roman Catholic. We had so much in common. And the other guy with whom I was the squad leader with whom I was close buddies for many, many months, he and I would go to church together and -- you know, so we could share that part of our lives. But all three of them were equally good friends. And you can find friends if you look for them. Sometimes, you know, you think, I'm going into a new situation, you know, all these strange, different people, you know, they're from different backgrounds and so forth, and maybe some of them have money, maybe some are very poor, and they have different habits, different likes and dislikes, but, you know, I found out from my military experience, you can go anywhere and you can find somebody who can be a friend with you, and so it's happened that way in life. You don't have to -- don't have to be selective. Things just sort of come automatically if you like certain people, get along with them. Yeah. Philosophize. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Very good. Think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: That's the basics, I think. There are many other stories.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Is there anything else? I have tape.

sp.speaker: Leslie Gordon Blasius
sp.p: Oh. Well, let me see. What have I been writing about, what I've been doing? Oh, I think you've hit most of the highlights.
